1: Copy Page
2: About LiveRamp Identity Resolution
3: Learn how to match data to RampIDs.
4: The Retrieval API allows you to resolve your data to individuals. To resolve raw PII data, you use the
5: Match endpoint
6: , and to resolve hashed PII data, you use the
7: Lookup endpoint
8: .
9: Rate Limits
10: API calls are made using
11: batch requests
12: , which allow you to send up to 360 calls per minute and 100-1000 records per call. The best practice is to batch the full 1000 records for as many calls as possible.
13: The Process
14: Request an access token.
15: Send your PII-based consumer data, such as name, address, phone number, or email address, to a RampID API Match or Lookup endpoint.
16: The API processes the request and then returns the applicable RampIDs along with any requested associated metadata.
17: If a matching set of touchpoints is found in the LiveRamp Identity Graph, the API returns a
18: maintained RampID
19: .  The Match endpoint may return multiple matches, but the Lookup matchpoint returns only a single RampID.
20: If a matching touchpoint isn't found, the API returns a
21: derived RampID
22: for each PII touchpoint.
23: For more information about maintained and derived RampIDs, see
24: RampIDs
25: .

1: Copy Page
2: About RampID Translation
3: Use the Translation endpoint to translate RampIDs from one partner encoding to another.
4: 📘
5: RampID translation was formerly known as "RampID transcoding". You might continue to see instances of "transcode", "transcoding", and "transcoded" in some places.
6: 🚧
7: Every RampID has a specific encoding to ensure the security and privacy of our partner's data. Due to the sensitive nature of RampIDs, certain privacy restrictions must be validated before translation access is provided. To enable this feature, contact your LiveRamp representative.
8: The API translates RampIDs from one partner encoding to another, enabling each partner to maintain control of their unique RampIDs in a secure collaboration.
9: Calls to translate RampIDs can be made as a single transaction call (for a single RampID) or as a batch request call (to translate up to 1,000 RampIDs per call).  We recommend you use batch requests whenever possible.
10: For more information, see "
11: Identity Translation
12: " in the Identity help.
13: RampID Structure
14: Each RampID consists of three parts:
15: The two-letter prefix, which denotes whether the RampID is maintained  (
16: XY
17: for individuals and
18: HY
19: for households) or derived (
20: Xi
21: or
22: Hi
23: for households)
24: The four-digit partner encoding (sometimes abbreviated to just "encoding"), which uniquely identifies the partner
25: The unique value that identifies the person or household
26: The default encoding for the RampIDs that you receive is called your "native encoding".
27: Other-to-Native Translation
28: When you receive RampIDs in encodings that are different from your default, you translate them to your native encoding.  Each partner encoding you would like to translate from requires an explicit one-time authorization to be performed by our client support team.
29: Once  this authorization is configured, you can send any RampID in any authorized encoding to the API and  then call the
30: /people/anonymousAbilitec/
31: endpoint (for individuals) or the
32: /households/anonymousAbilitec/
33: endpoint (for households) to receive that specific RampID in your native encoding.
34: Native-to-Other Translation
35: 📘
36: The ability to perform native-to-other translation requires proper authorization setup. Your LiveRamp representative will properly permission and provide partner encodings to you.
37: You can translate RampIDs from your native encoding to another entity's encoding by providing the partner encoding directly as a query parameter.
38: Requesting RampID Translation Permissions
39: Translation permissions depend on a two-way agreement between your company and the partner whose RampIDs you wish to translate. This agreement must explicitly consent to the translation while specifying the translation direction (native-to-other or other-to-native).
40: When you contact your LiveRamp representative about obtaining translation permissions, they will email both you and your partner to obtain this consent, cc:ing
41: [email protected]
42: .
43: The email for the partner doing the translation will read:
44: Please confirm permission to translate Company A RampIDs into Company 
45: B RampIDs.  Once received, your permission may be revoked at 
46: any time via email to
47: [email protected]
48: .
49: The email for the partner translated from will read:
50: Please confirm permission to translate Company A RampIDs into Company B RampIDs.  
51:  Once received, your permission may be revoked at any time via email to
52: [email protected]
53: .
54: If you are translating both to and from a partner's RampIDs, you must obtain separate permission for each translation direction:
55: Please confirm permission to translate Company A RampIDs into Company 
56: B RampIDs and to translate Company B RampIDs into 
57: Company A RampIDs.  Once received, your permission may be revoked at any time via 
58: email to
59: [email protected]

1: Copy Page
2: Identity Envelope Decryption
3: Learn how you can use the API for identity envelope decryption.
4: 📘
5: Want API reference information for  Identity Envelope Decryption?
6: See
7: Decrypt Identity Envelopes
8: for more information.
9: Due to the opaque nature of identity envelopes, they need to be decrypted into usable identifier data for the parties who receive them. The RampID API provides the decryption capability using the envelope decryption endpoint. This endpoint is used to decode and decrypt an envelope to extract the identifier in the envelope. The RampID API  then encrypts the value with a partner-specific encryption key and partner ID. The result is a RampID in the partner ID space that is usable for transactions.
10: There is a limitation to the type of data the API can decrypt from. The data represented in the envelopes must correspond to a valid RampID. Data types such as cookie and mobile ID are not currently supported.
11: Envelope Decryption Call
12: The API supports envelope lookups on
13: Person
14: -based identifiers. As the name implies, the input envelope must represent an individual in the underlying data, namely, with granularity of "X" (meaning INDIVIDUAL).
15: This endpoint supports POST operations with an envelope string passed in as a query parameter. The standard API parameters for the lookup endpoint are also applicable.
16: The URI path is:
17: /people/envelope?key=_\<envelope_string_representing_individual>_
18: The API returns status code 200 to indicate a successful execution. The resulting decrypted RampID is made available in the
19: anonymousConsumerLink
20: attribute in the "anonymousAbilitec" bundle.
21: 📘
22: Pseudonymous identifier
23: In the context of the RampID API, references to "anonymousAbilitec" indicate online device linking to match disparate devices to people-based pseudonymous identifiers. For more information, see "
24: RampID Methodology
25: " in the Identity documentation.
26: Unsuccessful responses from the endpoint may return status codes of 400 (bad request), 404 (not found) or 500 (server error). See
27: Errors and Troubleshooting
28: section for details.
29: 🚧
30: Before Using the Identity Envelope Decryption Endpoint
31: In order to use this endpoint, a user must be set up with proper credentials and access permissions. A client representative can help with this setup. For making API calls, a user needs to have a client ID and a client secret. For more details, see "
32: Request an Access Token
33: ".

1: Copy Page
2: Match Raw PII to RampID
3: post
4: https://us.identity.api.liveramp.com
5: /v1/batch/match
6: Use the Match endpoint to match raw PII data to a RampID.
7: You should use the Match endpoint when:
8: You want to match a file where the data have not been normalized.
9: You want to use fuzzy matching.
10: You have files with multiple PII columns.
11: When you send plaintext data to the Match endpoint, our algorithms perform data normalization and then use fuzzy matching when comparing the data to the LiveRamp Identity Graph. All PII fields in a particular record (such as name, address, ZIP code, phone number, or email address) are checked against the graph until a maintained RampID is found. If no maintained RampID is found, a derived RampID is returned. By default, the API returns a single RampID per PII record.
12: All calls to the Match endpoint must be structured as
13: batch request calls
14: . You can pass in up to 1000 URL strings in a single batch call.
15: 📘
16: See
17: RampIDs
18: for more information on maintained and derived RampIDs.
19: See
20: Requesting Multiple RampID Matching
21: for more information on matching a single PII record to multiple RampIDs.
22: Match Cascade
23: When you send plaintext PII to the Match endpoint, LiveRamp first uses data normalization to structure data variations (for example, in street types, such as "Boulevard" vs. "Blvd" vs. "Boulv") and then converts each component into a hash. We then use fuzzy matching to compare different combinations of the hashes to the data in the LiveRamp identity graph. The sequence in which the different combinations are tried is called a "match cascade.”
24: The match cascade determines not only the order or priority of the types of matches that are attempted, but also which steps are performed. For example, the obfuscated name, street address, and ZIP code are compared. If there isn't a match, the obfuscated name and email address are compared before moving on to the next steps in the match cascade. If a maintained RampID is not found after all the match cascade steps are performed, a derived RampID is returned.
25: When a match is found, LiveRamp returns a response that includes
26: insights and metadata
27: about how the match was obtained (that is, about which steps in the match cascade provided a RampID), as well as the RampID itself.
28: For more information, see "
29: Match Cascade
30: " in the Identity help.
31: Match Parameter Rules
32: The following list describes the general rules for calls to the Match endpoint.
33: Each URL string must start with
34: /people/match?
35: .
36: Match parameters must be included after the
37: ?
38: character in the URL string and formed as
39: [parameter_name]=[parameter_value]
40: .
41: Separate multiple parameters using
42: &
43: .
44: All calls must contain one or more match parameters in each URL string.
45: Do not include the parsed name (for example,
46: firstName
47: ,
48: middleName
49: , and
50: lastName
51: ) AND the unparsed name (
52: name
53: ) in the same request.
54: Do not include the parsed street address (for example,
55: primaryNumber
56: ,
57: street
58: ) AND the unparsed street address (
59: streetAddress
60: ) in the same request.
61: Match Parameter Validation
62: Variable
63: Rule
64: state
65: Must be the two-character uppercase state abbreviation
66: zipCode
67: Must be 5, 9, or 11 digits
68: email
69: Must contain an @ character and must contain a period (
70: .
71: ) in the domain portion
72: phone
73: Must be 10 digits with no special characters
74: limit
75: Must be an integer from 1 to 10. You can only specify an integer greater than 1 if you have the 1:1 permission. Contact your LiveRamp account representative for details
76: Match Parameter Combinations
77: Below are the most common input parameter combinations. Brackets (
78: [ ]
79: ) around a parameter indicates the parameter is optional.
80: Input Parameter Combination
81: Name + Street + [City] + [State] + ZipCode
82: Name + Email
83: Name + Phone
84: Email
85: Phone
86: Name + ZipCode

949: We retain Personal Data for as long as is necessary or as permitted in light of the purpose(s) for which it was obtained and consistent with applicable law, for example, for the purposes of satisfying any legal, regulatory, tax, accounting or reporting requirements. 950: The length of time we have an ongoing relationship with you and provide the Services to you (for example, for as long as you have an account with us or keep using the Services);
951: We are subject to legal obligation (for example, certain laws require us to keep records of your transactions for a certain period of time before we can delete them); or
952: Retention is advisable in light of our legal position (such as in regard to applicable statutes of limitations, litigation or regulatory investigations).
